findings.title: Batch is serialized after the buffer has already emptied it, so every audit event is lost
findings.scenario: EventBuffer.flush() calls this.write(this.items) and then right away runs this.items.length = 0 on the same array (event-buffer.js:15-16). The .then callback only runs on a later microtask. By then `events` is the emptied array, so events.map(toLine).join('') is '' and appendFile writes nothing. Every batch, including the one flushed on close, writes an empty string to the audit file.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The old sync writer serialized before flush() cleared the array. The new code delays serialization but never copies the array. There are no tests for the writer or the buffer.

findings.title: Write failures are only logged and flushAudit still resolves, so audit loss is silent
findings.scenario: With the default onError (console.error), a disk-full or permission error drops the batch after only a console line. flushAudit() on shutdown still resolves successfully. The old appendFileSync threw back to the caller.
findings.whyNotPrevented: This is a deliberate trade-off for background writes, but nothing reports the failure: no metric and no rejection from idle().

findings.title: Batch is turned into text later, after the buffer has already emptied the array, so every write is empty
findings.scenario: EventBuffer.flush() calls this.write(this.items) and then right away runs this.items.length = 0 (src/event-buffer.js:15-16). write() doesn't read `events` until the queued .then callback runs, which is after that line. By then the array is empty, so events.map(toLine).join('') is '' and appendFile writes nothing. Every audit event is lost, both on size-triggered flushes and on flushAudit at shutdown. If more events arrive first, the same array may instead hold later events by the time it is read, so batches can be written under the wrong flush or more than once.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The old sync version read the array before flush cleared it. The new code captures the array reference, not a copy. There are no tests in the repo.

findings.title: Failed audit writes are now logged and dropped instead of reaching anyone
findings.scenario: Disk full or a permissions error: before, appendFileSync threw inside the request (or onClose), so the failure showed up. Now the batch is logged with console.error and thrown away, and flushAudit() resolves normally, so shutdown reports success even though audit records were lost.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The catch handles every error with no retry and no way for idle() to report failure.

findings.title: Write queue has no size limit
findings.scenario: If the disk is slow or stalled and traffic stays high, closures holding event batches keep piling up on the promise chain. Memory grows with nothing pushing back and no cap.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing limits how many writes can wait in the queue.

The events.map(toLine) inside .then runs on a later microtask, when the array is already empty, so appendFile writes ''. Every audit event is silently lost, both for batch-size flushes and on shutdown. Before this change appendFileSync serialized the array before it was cleared.

findings.scenario: If the disk is full or permissions are wrong, each batch is logged to console.error and thrown away. flushAudit() still resolves successfully, so shutdown code cannot tell that audit data was lost. Before this change the sync error went back to the caller.

findings.title: New async ordering and flush behaviour has no tests

findings.title: Flags left unset become explicit undefined and replace every default
findings.scenario: Running the CLI with no flags makes cli.js pass { baseUrl: undefined, retries: undefined, timeoutMs: undefined }. Object spread copies keys whose value is undefined, so all three defaults are replaced. With retries undefined, `0 <= undefined` is false, so the loop never runs and get() throws undefined. Even if it did run, the URL would be 'undefined/status' and AbortSignal.timeout(undefined) would throw a TypeError. So the default call no longer works, which goes against the goal of keeping the current defaults.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test runs the CLI or createClient with options that are partly undefined, and the spread hides the problem.

findings.title: Non-numeric --retries or --timeout is not rejected and turns into NaN
findings.scenario: `--retries abc` gives NaN, so the retry loop runs zero times and the CLI throws `undefined` without any message. `--timeout abc` passes NaN to AbortSignal.timeout, which throws a TypeError. `--retries ''` becomes 0 without any warning.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The input is never validated after Number(), and no test covers bad flag values.

findings.title: createClient's positional signature changed, so fetchImpl moved to the second argument
findings.scenario: Any caller or future test that passes a fake fetch as the first argument, as the old signature expected, would now have it spread into config and fall back to the real global fetch. No such caller exists in the repo today.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No tests inject fetchImpl, so nothing catches the change in argument order.

findings.title: Entries at exactly UTC midnight are counted in two days and twice in the range total
findings.scenario: Ledger.entriesBetween keeps entries where `at >= from && at <= to`, so both ends are included. An entry at exactly 2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z shows up in the 2026-03-01 row and again in the 2026-03-02 row. Because the range total adds up the rows, that entry is counted twice there too. Midnight is a common time for batch or renewal charges, so this will happen.
findings.whyNotPrevented: dayStatement avoids the overlap by ending each day at endOfDay (start + DAY_MS - 1). The new code uses the next day's start as the upper bound instead. There are no tests for the report.

findings.title: No limit on the size of the date range
findings.scenario: A request like GET /reports/revenue?from=0001-01-01&to=9999-12-31 makes dailyRevenue loop about 3.65 million times. Each pass runs a full linear filter over every ledger entry, and the response has millions of rows. One request can block the event loop.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The validation only checks that the dates parse and that from < to. It never checks the span.

findings.title: 'to' is exclusive, so the last named day is left out and a one-day report is rejected
findings.scenario: from=2026-03-01&to=2026-03-31 returns only 30 rows and leaves out March 31. from=2026-03-01&to=2026-03-01 returns a 400 error. Callers have to know to pass the day after the last day they want. The error message does not say this.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The range semantics are not documented, and no test pins down the expected behavior.

findings.title: The new report and route have no tests
findings.scenario: None of these are covered: the midnight boundary double count, an empty range, or the range total matching the sum of the entries.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The repo has no test files, and the diff adds none.

findings.title: Midnight entries are counted in two days because the ledger's end bound is inclusive
findings.scenario: `Ledger.entriesBetween` keeps entries where `at >= from && at <= to`, so both ends count. `chargeRenewal` records every renewal at exactly `startOfDay(periodStart)`, which is 00:00:00Z. A renewal on 2026-03-02 is therefore counted in the 2026-03-01 row and again in the 2026-03-02 row. The range total sums the rows, so it counts every renewal twice. Also, a renewal at exactly `to` (the day the report leaves out) still appears in the last row, so revenue from outside the range gets into the report.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `dayStatement` avoids this by ending at `endOfDay(day)` (next midnight minus 1 ms). The new code ends at next midnight instead, and no test covers entries at midnight.

findings.title: `to` is exclusive, so the last date is dropped and a one-day report is impossible
findings.scenario: `from=2026-01-01&to=2026-01-31` returns rows only up to 2026-01-30, because the loop runs while `day < to`. `from=2026-01-31&to=2026-01-31` is rejected with 400. A caller would normally read a YYYY-MM-DD range as including both dates, so January 31 revenue goes missing without any error.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The error message and the code don't say whether `to` is inclusive or exclusive, and no test pins the boundary down.

findings.title: No limit on range length; each day scans the whole ledger
findings.quote: return { status: 200, body: dailyRevenue(ledger, from, to) };
findings.scenario: `from=0001-01-01&to=9999-12-31` loops about 3.65 million days, filtering the full ledger each day, and builds a response with millions of rows. One request can tie up the server.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The route checks the date format and order but not how long the range is.

findings.title: Invalid calendar dates like 2026-02-30 are accepted and silently rolled over
findings.scenario: Some JS engines turn `2026-02-30` into March 2 instead of NaN, so the 400 check does not catch it. The report then covers dates the caller didn't ask for.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The only check is for NaN, and the parsed date is never compared back to the input text.

findings.title: Midnight entries are counted on two days, so day totals and the range total come out too high
findings.scenario: Ledger.entriesBetween includes both ends (entry.at >= from && entry.at <= to). The window for each day ends at the next midnight, and that midnight is also the start of the next day's window. chargeRenewal always records renewals at startOfDay(periodStart), which is exactly midnight. So when a renewal falls on any day after the first one in the range, it is added to both the day before and its own day. The range total is the sum of the rows, so it counts that renewal twice too.
findings.whyNotPrevented: dayStatement avoids this by using endOfDay (midnight minus 1 ms). The new code uses addDays(day, 1) instead. No test covers entries at midnight.

findings.title: The `to` date is left out, so a one-day report needs to = the next day
findings.scenario: GET /reports/revenue?from=2026-10-01&to=2026-10-31 returns no row for Oct 31 (the loop runs while day < to). from=to=2026-10-01 is rejected with 400. Most callers would expect both dates in the range to be included. Neither the error message nor any docs say the end is exclusive.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The range rules aren't documented and there are no tests.

findings.title: No limit on range length, and each day scans the whole ledger
findings.quote: return { status: 200, body: dailyRevenue(ledger, from, to) };
findings.scenario: from=1970-01-01&to=9999-12-31 produces about 2.9M loop iterations. Each one filters every ledger entry, so the cost is O(days × entries) and one request can tie up the server.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The route doesn't validate the maximum span.

findings.title: parseDate accepts inputs that aren't plain YYYY-MM-DD
findings.scenario: If the from query param is missing, the string becomes 'undefinedT00:00:00Z' and returns 400, which is fine. But engines may accept loose formats like '2026-10' through Date.parse, and the input isn't checked against a strict pattern.
findings.whyNotPrevented: There's no regex check on the input format.

findings.title: The new report and route have no tests
findings.scenario: There are no tests for day boundaries, midnight renewals, inclusive vs. exclusive range ends, or validation errors. That's how the double-counting bug got through.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The diff doesn't add any tests.

findings.title: Attempt key uses the raw email, so changing case or adding spaces skips the limit
findings.scenario: An attacker sends 5 guesses for victim@x.com, then 5 for Victim@x.com, 5 for ' victim@x.com', and so on. Each variant gets its own rate-limit counter, but users.findByEmail normalizes them all (trim + lowercase) to the same account. That allows nearly unlimited password guesses against one account. A successful login also only resets the counter for the exact spelling used.
findings.whyNotPrevented: UserStore normalizes emails inside findByEmail. The limiter key is built before that and never goes through normalizeEmail. No tests cover login rate limiting.

findings.title: Login limiter map grows without limit, one entry per email ever tried
findings.quote: const loginAttempts = new RateLimiter({ limit: 5, windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000 });
findings.scenario: RateLimiter only drops an entry on reset(), which needs a successful login. It never removes expired windows. Requests with random or made-up emails (which can never log in) each leave a permanent Map entry, so memory keeps growing on a public, unauthenticated endpoint.
findings.whyNotPrevented: RateLimiter has no eviction. The password-reset limiter is keyed by IP, which limits growth. This one is keyed by an email the attacker chooses.

findings.title: No tests for the new lockout or the reset on success
findings.scenario: Nothing checks that the 6th attempt within 15 minutes gets 429, that a successful login clears the count, or that email variants share one counter. A test for that last case would have caught the bypass above.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The repo has no test files.

findings.title: Limiter key uses the raw email, but account lookup normalizes it, so the limit is easy to get around
findings.scenario: An attacker gets 5 guesses with 'alice@x.com', then 5 more with 'Alice@x.com', 'ALICE@x.com', ' alice@x.com' and so on. UserStore.findByEmail runs normalizeEmail (trim + toLowerCase), so every variant hits the same account while each one gets its own fresh limiter bucket. In practice the per-account guess limit is unlimited.

findings.title: Login limiter map grows without bound because any email string creates an entry
findings.quote: const loginAttempts = new RateLimiter({ limit: 5, windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000 });
findings.scenario: RateLimiter.allow adds a Map entry for every new key and never removes old windows. It only deletes on reset, which needs a successful login. An unauthenticated client can POST /login with millions of random or nonexistent emails and keep growing process memory.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The reset limiter has the same design, but it is keyed by IP, which limits how many keys exist. This one is keyed by arbitrary user input, and nothing caps or prunes it.

findings.title: Anyone can lock out any known account
findings.scenario: The check runs before the password is verified and is keyed only by account. An attacker who sends 5 bad attempts every 15 minutes keeps the real user locked out, and even the correct password gets a 429.
findings.whyNotPrevented: This follows from the per-account design the author asked for. There is no per-IP part to the key and no way for the real user to recover access.

findings.title: No tests cover the new login limit or the reset on success
findings.scenario: A regression such as the normalization bypass above, or an off-by-one at the 5-attempt boundary, would not be caught.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The repository has no test directory.

findings.title: Stock is taken off before the order status is saved, so a failure in between loses stock
findings.scenario: If reserveStock fails partway through its Promise.all of stock.set calls, or orders.set(orderId, next) throws, some or all stock is already gone while the order stays 'pending'. The worker logs the error and moves on, so that stock never comes back. If the job were ever retried, the order would reserve stock a second time.

findings.title: The missing-account path never releases the payout lock
findings.quote: throw new PayoutError(`payout ${payoutId} has no bank account`);
findings.scenario: A payout with no accountNumber gets the lock `payout:<id>`, is marked failed, and then the code throws before reaching the try/finally that calls release(). The lock stays held, so any later sendPayout for that id (for example a retry after the account is added) hangs or deadlocks. If payouts.get or payouts.update throws, the lock is also leaked, because the get call was moved out of the try block too.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The new early return/throw and the moved payouts.get call both sit between acquire() and the try block whose finally calls release().

findings.scenario: Suppose a payout already has status 'sent' and its accountNumber was later cleared, for example because the account was removed. Calling it again (a retry or duplicate job) now writes status 'failed' over the sent record and throws. Before this change it would return early as already sent.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The account check runs before the existing `status === 'sent'` idempotency check.

findings.whyNotPrevented: The worker has no branch for permanent PayoutError failures, and the diff doesn't touch worker.js.

findings.title: Refund moves money from the customer to the store
findings.scenario: Support refunds a 5000-cent order. `transfer(to, from, amount)` takes the destination first, so the customer's balance drops by 5000 and the store's goes up by 5000. The customer is charged again when they should be paid back.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The argument order in `transfer(toAccountId, fromAccountId, …)` in `src/ledger.js` is easy to get backwards, and nothing tests that a refund lowers the store balance and raises the customer's. `payouts.js` uses the right order (`transfer(seller.accountId, STORE_ACCOUNT, …)`), and this code reverses it.

findings.title: Repeated partial refunds can add up to more than the order total

findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing records how much of an order has already been refunded. The check only compares one request with the original total.

findings.title: Order total and destination account come straight from the request body

other.title: Every error is retried, including permanent ones

findings.title: Upload failure is swallowed after the last retry, so the local report gets deleted without ever being archived
findings.quote: await retry(() => bucket.put(key, body, { contentType: 'application/x-ndjson' }), { attempts: 3, label: `upload ${key}` });
findings.scenario: Storage is down for longer than the retry window (about 200ms + 400ms). All 3 puts fail. On the last attempt, retry() calls `return report(error, ...)`, which logs the error and returns undefined instead of throwing. uploadArchive then returns the key as if the upload worked. archiveDay goes on to `unlink(file)` and deletes the only copy of that day's ndjson. runNightly counts the day as archived, and the metrics overstate reports.archived. Before this change, the error from bucket.put would have propagated, the unlink would have been skipped, and the file would have stayed on disk for the next run.
findings.whyNotPrevented: retry.js treats running out of attempts as best-effort: it reports and resolves. That is fine for the existing metrics caller but not for an upload whose success decides whether a delete runs. The diff doesn't change that behaviour or rethrow, and there are no tests around archive failure.

findings.title: Total retry window is too short for a 'brief storage outage'
findings.scenario: Because delayMs defaults to 200 with linear backoff, the 3 attempts span only about 600ms. Most short storage outages or throttling episodes last seconds, so the nightly run would still fail (or, given the bug above, silently lose data) in exactly the case the author is targeting.
findings.whyNotPrevented: delayMs isn't passed, so the default meant for metrics is used.

findings.title: Every error is retried, including permanent ones
findings.scenario: Auth, permission or bad-bucket errors are retried 3 times with sleeps before failing. This adds delay and log noise without any chance of success.
findings.whyNotPrevented: retry() has no predicate for which errors are retryable.

findings.title: Out-of-order responses can overwrite newer results with stale ones
findings.quote:
const products = await searchProducts(term);
    renderResults(list, products);
findings.scenario: The user types 'sho', pauses, then types 'shoes'. If the 'sho' request finishes after the 'shoes' request, the list shows results for 'sho' while the box says 'shoes'. The same happens when the user clears the box to under 2 characters: the list is emptied, then a request still in flight fills it again with old results.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The debounce only delays when requests start. Nothing cancels an in-flight request (no AbortController) or checks that a response matches the latest term before rendering it. Typing as you go makes overlapping requests common, while the old Enter-only flow rarely had them.

findings.title: Enter no longer searches, and 1-character searches are now impossible
findings.scenario: Before this change, pressing Enter ran the search right away for any term, including a single character. Now Enter does nothing, the user waits for the 200ms pause, and terms shorter than 2 characters can never be searched.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The submit handler was reduced to preventDefault, and MIN_TERM_LENGTH applies on every path with no Enter fallback that searches immediately.

findings.title: A failed search causes an unhandled promise rejection on every pause
findings.scenario: When the API returns a non-OK status, searchProducts throws. The debounced async callback is called from setTimeout and nothing awaits it, so each typing pause produces an unhandled rejection and the list keeps showing stale results with no error state.
findings.whyNotPrevented: There is no try/catch around the call. The old submit handler had the same gap, but it only ran on Enter. Now it runs on every pause in typing.

findings.title: Slow older responses can overwrite newer results
findings.scenario: The user types 'sho', pauses, then types 'shoes'. If the 'sho' request comes back after the 'shoes' request, renderResults shows results for 'sho' while the box says 'shoes'. findings.title: Shared defaults object is changed in place, so one user's preferences show up for other users
findings.scenario: defaultPreferences() returns the same DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object on every call (src/defaults.js:8). The loop writes saved values straight into that object. Say user A has saved theme 'dark'. After A's request, the shared defaults now say theme 'dark'. User B has nothing saved, so B is shown 'dark' too. This also means every response returns the same object, which is the same live module state.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaults.js hands back the constant instead of a copy, and no test fetches two users with different saved preferences

findings.title: `in` check accepts inherited keys like __proto__, constructor and toString
findings.scenario: `in` also finds keys inherited from Object.prototype. Saved preferences parsed from JSON can contain __proto__ or toString as normal keys. These pass the check: assigning __proto__ swaps the result object's prototype, and toString or constructor gets written into the response. The intent was to drop unsupported keys, and these are not dropped. Use Object.hasOwn(defaults, key) instead.
findings.whyNotPrevented: no test sends saved keys that are not supported, including keys from the prototype

findings.title: Writes saved preferences into the shared defaults object, so one user's values leak to everyone
findings.scenario: `defaultPreferences()` in src/defaults.js returns the same `DEFAULT_PREFERENCES` object on every call, not a copy. User A has `{theme:'dark'}` saved, and `getUser(A)` sets `DEFAULT_PREFERENCES.theme = 'dark'`. User B has nothing saved, and `getUser(B)` then also returns `theme: 'dark'`. The defaults stay changed for the rest of the process. Every response body also points at that one shared object, so changing it later changes responses that were already built.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The code assumes `defaultPreferences()` returns a new object, but it hands back the module-level constant. There are no tests in the repo, and a test with only one user would not catch this. Fix: copy it (`{ ...defaultPreferences() }`), or have defaults.js return a copy.

findings.title: The `in` check also accepts inherited keys such as `__proto__`, `constructor` and `toString`, so some unsupported keys are not ignored
findings.scenario: The saved preferences come from `JSON.parse`, so a stored `{"constructor":"x"}` or `{"toString":1}` passes `key in preferences` and gets added to the response, even though it is not a supported key. A stored `{"__proto__":{...}}` becomes a real own key after `JSON.parse`, so it also passes the check. Assigning it then replaces the prototype of the (shared) preferences object, and inherited properties can show up on later lookups.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` looks at the prototype chain, not just the supported keys. Use `Object.hasOwn(defaults, key)`, or check against a fixed list of allowed keys.
